Battle of Pharsalus. In 48 BC near the city of Pharsalus in Thessaly, Greece, Julius Caesar crushed the forces of Pompey the Great, establishing himself as Rome's undisputed leader and paving the way for the end of the Republic.

Caesar commanded approximately 23,000 legionaries, while Pompey mustered roughly 45,000 soldiers, including substantial cavalry and allied forces loyal to the optimates faction. Pompey's superior numbers and cavalry led him to expect an easy victory.

But Caesar's tight discipline and unconventional tactics proved decisive. He positioned his right flank obliquely and held a cavalry reserve hidden from view to counter Pompey's mounted forces. When Pompey's cavalry charged, Caesar's hidden cavalry and cohorts destroyed them completely, then wheeled to attack Pompey's infantry from the flank and rear.

Pompey's army could not withstand this assault. It collapsed entirely. Pompey himself fled, eventually making his way to Egypt where the Egyptian king had him assassinated.

Caesar's victory made him dictator and effectively ended the optimates' power. But his dominance did not last long. His subsequent assassination sparked another civil war that would bring a new generation of leaders to prominence. Among those who rose to power in the chaos Caesar unleashed was Octavian, who would eventually become the first emperor. The man Pompey had once dominated the Mediterranean, but his defeat at Pharsalus showed that even his once-invincible reputation could be overcome by a brilliant and determined rival.
